brief.greeting: Good morning. LLMs are still asking for evidence before they can call a clinical mistake safe.

stories.headline: LLM judges need evidence to flag unsafe actions
stories.body: **Only with proof:** Researchers fed 416 faulty clinical trajectories to open-weight LLM judges and found they missed errors unless the prompt included concrete evidence. Without it, the models left the final answer unchanged.
stories.why: Your AI pipeline must surface raw data, not just conclusions, to catch hidden hazards.

stories.headline: Claude restores 4‑bit CNN accuracy
stories.body: **Tool‑free repair:** A frontier Claude model rewrote weights of a 20k‑parameter CIFAR‑10 CNN, lifting 4‑bit quantized test accuracy from 60.4% back toward the original 81.4% without external tools.
stories.why: You can keep model size low while preserving performance, saving memory on edge devices.

stories.headline: Tiny edits boost small model math scores
stories.body: **Gradient nudges:** Fine‑tuning just 140 k weights of the 0.8B Qwen3.5 model raised its MATH‑500 reasoning accuracy from 15.4% to 45.5% using 50 examples in minutes.
stories.why: Small, targeted edits can dramatically improve reasoning without full retraining.

highlights.title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
highlights.summary: LLM judges only reliably detect unsafe clinical actions when provided with clinical evidence; without it they cannot spot errors that leave the final answer unchanged.
highlights.detail: The study used MedAgentBench to inject controlled errors into verified agent trajectories and compared judges' assessments against correct counterparts. Judges showed higher reliability when they could reference the underlying clinical evidence rather than just the agent's final output. This highlights a limitation of current LLM-based safety evaluation in clinical AI.

highlights.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
highlights.summary: A frontier Claude LLM can recover most of the accuracy lost by 4‑bit quantization of a 20k‑parameter CIFAR‑10 CNN, boosting test performance toward the original 81.4% level.
highlights.detail: The experiment gave the LLM the full float weights as text and asked it to produce a 4‑bit network without running inference. Four evaluation protocols tested whether the model applied optimizations beyond simple rounding. The best LLM answer (Opus 5.5) raised accuracy substantially, demonstrating that language models can perform non‑trivial weight‑space programming.

highlights.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
highlights.summary: Fine‑tuning ~140 k weights of Qwen3.5‑0.8B with gradient edits raises MATH‑500 thinking‑mode accuracy from 15.4% to up to 45.5% using only 50 examples in a few minutes.
highlights.detail: The edit targets the largest gradients on the model's own correct answers, concentrating changes on the most constant channel of the first three layers. Training on a single GPU for 2‑9 minutes suffices, while random edits to 1,398 positions only reach 16.3% accuracy, showing the importance of gradient‑guided selection. This complements larger weight‑space edits from frontier models.

highlights.detail: Vx treats each machine as a source file of declarations, allowing types to specify the memory tier (e.g., host, device) and function signatures to serve as complete contracts. The language aims for scalability across CPUs, GPUs, and heterogeneous cores, with optional compiler checks for safety properties. GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
items.summary: GPT‑6 models can design protein structures and sequences, and laboratory tests reported binding evidence across five different targets.
items.detail: The models generate both structural predictions and amino‑acid sequences using internal reasoning and code generation capabilities. Experimental validation confirmed functional interactions, suggesting that large language models can contribute to protein engineering workflows without specialized training.

items.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
items.summary: LLM agents are primarily designed to serve the interests of the companies that deploy them rather than end users.
items.detail: The article argues that the incentive structures behind commercial LLM deployments favor corporate goals such as data collection, brand reinforcement, and revenue generation, which can limit the autonomy and usefulness of agents for individual users.

items.title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
items.summary: Two amateur astronomers used Codex and the Astra tool to analyze NASA Kepler and TESS data, identifying candidate exoplanets.
items.detail: By leveraging Codex for code generation and Astra for data processing, the astronomers processed public light‑curve archives, demonstrating that hobbyist‑level AI tools can contribute to the discovery pipeline for distant worlds.

items.title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
items.summary: The Microduck project demonstrates a Sim2Real obstacle‑avoidance pipeline using Isaac Lab for simulation and Newton for real‑world deployment.
items.detail: The workflow shows how simulated training in Isaac Lab can be transferred to a physical Microduck robot via the Newton framework, reducing the need for manual tuning and enabling rapid iteration on navigation algorithms.

items.title: Model: llamaindex/OCRia-nano-1
items.summary: The llamaindex/OCRia-nano-1 model is an image‑to‑text system that has been downloaded 126 times and received 193 likes on Hugging Face.
items.detail: Designed for lightweight OCR tasks, the model targets edge devices and integrates with the LlamaIndex ecosystem, offering a compact alternative to larger vision‑language models.

items.title: Security updates for Tuesday
items.summary: Tuesday’s security update cycle released patches for numerous packages across AlmaLinux, Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, and Oracle Linux.
items.detail: The updates address vulnerabilities in core components such as the kernel, OpenSSH, curl, and graphics libraries, and are distributed through each distribution’s regular package repositories.

items.title: Firefox 161.0 released
items.summary: Firefox 161.0 was released, adding a shortcut for copying the current tab’s URL, a Tab Groups menu item, and per‑site VPN toggling.
items.detail: The update also includes a batch of security fixes and minor UI tweaks, continuing Mozilla’s monthly release cadence while expanding user‑customizable privacy controls.

items.title: A Switchboard Operator Simulator, On Real Hardware
items.summary: Hackaday published a feature describing a Switchboard Operator Simulator that runs on actual vintage hardware.
items.detail: The article explores how the simulator recreates the experience of operating a telephone switchboard using period-accurate components, highlighting challenges of interfacing modern software with legacy electromechanical systems. It also notes the educational value for hardware hobbyists interested in retro computing.

items.title: Ask Hackaday: Putting the C in CPU
items.summary: Hackaday ran a column titled “Ask Hackaday: Putting the C in CPU” where a contributor shared a hobby involving low‑level CPU design.
items.detail: The piece recounts a personal anecdote from a meeting where the author described building a simple CPU from scratch using C‑style abstractions, illustrating how hobbyist projects can intersect with professional engineering discussions. It emphasizes hands‑on learning of instruction set architecture.

items.title: Keeping your Molten Salt Reactor Fuel Fresh with Helium Bubbles
items.summary: Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute reported a method using helium bubbles to keep molten‑salt reactor fuel clean.
items.detail: The technique injects helium micro‑bubbles into the reactor core, which rise and capture contaminants, reducing fouling without interrupting operation. The study, currently behind a paywall, suggests potential for longer fuel cycles and lower maintenance in next‑generation reactors.

items.title: The 3D Printer Scam Targeting UK Hackerspaces
items.summary: Hackaday warned readers about a 3D‑printer scam targeting UK hackerspaces that promises discounted printers but delivers non‑functional units.
items.detail: The article outlines how the fraudsters use professional‑looking websites and limited‑time offers to lure groups into pre‑paying for equipment that never arrives or is substandard. It provides steps for verification and advice on reporting such scams to authorities.

items.title: Vx: A Programming Language for Scalable, Maintainable and Secure Systems
items.summary: The arXiv paper introduces Vx, a systems programming language designed to express memory location and concurrency contracts directly in code.
items.detail: Vx treats each machine as a source file of declarations, allowing types to specify the memory tier (e.g., host, device) and function signatures to serve as complete contracts. The language aims for scalability across CPUs, GPUs, and heterogeneous cores, with optional compiler checks for safety properties. The report details six design principles and showcases examples of secure, maintainable code.

items.title: Estimating GPU Roofline Arithmetic Intensity with Off-the-Shelf LLMs and Compiler Artifacts
items.summary: An arXiv study evaluates off‑the‑shelf LLMs for estimating GPU Roofline arithmetic intensity, finding compiler artifacts improve accuracy.
items.detail: The authors tested three models—deepseek‑v4‑flash, gemini‑3.7‑flash, and gpt‑5.6‑sol—across five kernel families, four GPUs (NVIDIA and AMD), and four runtimes (CUDA, HIP, OpenMP, OpenCL). Providing compiler intermediate representations raised the proportion of estimates within a 20% error margin from roughly 10% to 30%, enhancing correct bandwidth‑bound versus compute‑bound classification.

items.title: Verifying Type Soundness for Nontransitive Information Flow Security
items.summary: A machine‑checked soundness proof of a type system for nontransitive noninterference (NTNI) in an imperative language was completed using Dafny, the first such formal verification for NTNI enforcement.
items.detail: The original NTNI formulation targeted functional languages with memory operators, and later extensions lacked a high‑assurance proof. This work bridges that gap, confirming that the type‑enforced NTNI mechanism correctly enforces the security property.

items.title: Concurrent Visibility: Higher-Order Concurrency with First-Order Store
items.summary: An operational game semantics for a call‑by‑value concurrent higher‑order language with first‑order store is introduced, defining a complete‑trace preorder and proving its soundness for the contextual preorder.
items.detail: The semantics adapts the visibility concept from sequential languages to concurrency, handling references that may contain other references or primitive values but not functions. Completeness is shown for the fragment where functions return first‑order values, and a synchronization‑based composition underpins the adequacy proof.

items.title: Blockchain-IoT Convergence for Spatiotemporal Data Systems: Challenges, Solutions, and Research Gaps
items.summary: The paper outlines how blockchain combined with IoT indexing can improve authenticity, accuracy, and real‑time processing of spatiotemporal data collected from large sensor networks.
items.detail: By leveraging blockchain’s decentralized consensus, the approach aims to prevent data fabrication and single points of failure while enabling efficient spatiotemporal indexing for quick retrieval. The authors review existing literature and identify gaps for future research on scalable indexing and query mechanisms in blockchain‑IoT systems.

items.title: Parallel Memory Management in Goose, C++, and Rust: An Experimental Study of Allocation, Reclamation, and Scaling
items.summary: Goose v2026.3 achieved up to 10.95% lower median execution time than C++ on depth‑20 binary trees using eight parallel workers.
items.detail: The study compared Goose against C++ and Rust implementations across dynamic arrays and binary trees on a 4‑core/8‑thread workstation. Measurements included whole‑process time, release intervals, and memory usage, with strong and weak scaling analyses confirming Goose’s advantage in parallel memory management.

items.title: pytorch/torchtitan
items.summary: pytorch/torchtitan is a PyTorch‑native platform designed for training generative AI models.
items.detail: The repository provides integrated tooling and optimizations that streamline large‑scale model training workflows within the PyTorch ecosystem, targeting researchers and engineers building generative systems.

items.title: ruffle-rs/ruffle
items.summary: ruffle-rs/ruffle is a Flash Player emulator implemented in Rust.
items.detail: The project aims to preserve legacy Flash content by re‑creating the runtime environment with Rust’s safety and performance guarantees, offering a modern, open‑source alternative to the discontinued Adobe Flash Player.

items.title: rustdesk/rustdesk
items.summary: rustdesk is an open-source remote desktop application that can be self‑hosted, offering a self‑managed alternative to TeamViewer.
items.detail: The software supports cross‑platform connections and aims to give users full control over their data and infrastructure. It is written in Rust, emphasizing performance and security, and can be deployed on personal servers without third‑party services.

items.title: superdesigndev/treg
items.summary: treg provides an OpenRouter interface for building agent tools, with community support via a Discord server.
items.detail: The Python library simplifies integration of large language model routing into autonomous agents. It includes example configurations and encourages collaboration through its Discord community, facilitating rapid prototyping of AI‑driven workflows.

items.title: toeverything/AFFiNE
items.summary: AFFiNE is an open‑source, privacy‑first knowledge‑base platform that combines planning, sorting, and creation features beyond tools like Notion and Miro.
items.detail: Designed for extensibility, AFFiNE offers customizable workspaces and real‑time collaboration while keeping data under user control. It targets users who need integrated documentation, brainstorming, and project management in a single, self‑hosted solution.

items.title: vllm-project/vllm-ascend
items.summary: vllm‑ascend is a community‑maintained plugin enabling vLLM to run on Huawei Ascend AI hardware.
items.detail: The Python plugin adapts the high‑throughput inference engine vLLM for Ascend's accelerator architecture, expanding hardware compatibility for large language model serving. It is open source and aims to provide performance parity with GPU deployments.
